passages.happening:
‘The hand of the LORD was upon me, and He brought me out by His Spirit and set me down in the middle of the valley, and it was full of bones’ (verse 1). They were very many, ‘and indeed, they were very dry’ (verse 2). ‘Son of man, can these bones come to life?’ God asks. Ezekiel answers that only God knows (verse 3).

God tells him to prophesy to the bones. As he does, there is a rattling, and the bones come together, ‘bone to bone’ (verse 7). Tendons, flesh and skin cover them, ‘but there was no breath in them’ (verse 8). Then God tells him to prophesy to the breath: “Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe into these slain, so that they may live!” (verse 9). He prophesied, ‘and the breath entered them, and they came to life and stood on their feet’, a vast army (verse 10).

God explains: ‘these bones are the whole house of Israel’, who say their bones are dried up, their hope is gone and they are cut off (verse 11). ‘O My people, I will open your graves and bring you up from them, and I will bring you back to the land of Israel’ (verse 12). ‘I will put My Spirit in you and you will live’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The vision belongs to the time after Jerusalem's fall, when the exiles' hope had collapsed. To lie unburied was one of the worst fates imaginable, a mark of defeat and curse. These bones are the slain, a defeated army left to bleach in the sun, long dead and past any natural hope. For a priest, bones were also the strongest source of ritual uncleanness, which makes Ezekiel's walk among them more striking.

One Hebrew word, ruach, carries the chapter. It means spirit (verse 1), breath (verses 5 to 10), the winds (verse 9) and God's Spirit (verse 14). The scene echoes creation, when God formed the man from dust and breathed into him the breath of life.
passages.later: At creation God ‘breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being’ (Genesis 2:7). Isaiah said, ‘Your dead will live; their bodies will rise’ (Isaiah 26:19).
passages.hard:
Is this chapter about the resurrection of the dead, or only about Israel's return from exile?

In its own setting the vision is explained as a picture of the nation's revival: the bones are the whole house of Israel, their graves are the exile, and their rising is the return to the land (verses 11 to 14). Most scholars read it first as a picture of national restoration, and note that the Old Testament's fuller hope of bodily resurrection appears more plainly later, in Daniel 12:2.

Yet the picture only works because resurrection was imaginable as something God could do, and later Jewish and Christian readers took it to point to the resurrection of the dead as well; rabbinic discussion in the Talmud debated whether the dead Ezekiel saw were actually raised. Many Christians read the chapter on two levels: it promises the restoration of God's people, and it looks toward the bodily resurrection that the New Testament grounds in Christ's own rising. The New Testament does not quote this chapter, so that second level is a reading. Both readings agree that only God's word and Spirit can give life to what is dead.
passages.asks: Ezekiel answered God's question honestly: only God knew. Ask what in your life, or in someone you love, looks like dry bones. And ask whether you can bring it to God and say the same.

passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to take one stick and write on it for Judah, and another for Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and the house of Israel with him. ‘Then join them together into one stick, so that they become one in your hand’ (verse 17). When people ask what it means, he is to say that God will make Israel and Judah one stick in his hand (verses 18-19).

‘I will make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel, and one king will rule over all of them’ (verse 22). They will no longer defile themselves with idols, and God will cleanse them (verse 23). ‘My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them’ (verse 24). ‘And I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant’ (verse 26). ‘My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The kingdom split about 930 BC, when the northern tribes rejected Solomon's son Rehoboam. The northern kingdom, often called Israel, Ephraim or Joseph after its leading tribe, fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and its people were deported. Now Judah too was in exile. Joining the stick of Joseph to the stick of Judah promises more than the return of the recent exiles: it promises all twelve tribes as one people again, long after the north had disappeared.

Writing names on rods was a known practice; Moses once wrote each tribe's name on a staff. Dwelling place recalls the tabernacle, where God lived among his people in the wilderness.
passages.later: God promised at Sinai, ‘I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people’ (Leviticus 26:12). Hosea foresaw Judah and Israel gathered under one leader (Hosea 1:11).
passages.asks: God promised to make two divided peoples one in his hand. Ask where there is division in your family or church that seems permanent. And ask what part you could play in its healing.
